# Phase 10 gate report: long-document perplexity, and how little it sees

**Status: complete. The gate deliverables are done (tests, experiment, this report, commit).**

Brief §B7 lists four quality measurements in order of cost. Phases 1-9 ran the first two
(teacher-forced divergence, and NIAH retrieval); the third, **perplexity on long documents,
reported per context length**, was never run. This phase runs it for rungs 2, 4, 5 and 8 at every
budget in the sweep and at 4 context lengths.

It was also chosen for a practical reason: it is a quality measurement, run on the deterministic
kernel, so unlike a timing run nothing else on the machine can move its numbers.

## Gate checklist (CLAUDE.md rule 3)

- [x] **Tests run.** `pytest`, all passing. New: `tests/test_perplexity.py` pins the fixed-target
  windows (the same tokens are scored at every context, and a target without room for its context
  is refused), the NLL read-out (both comparison paths agree, and a self-comparison reports the
  reference's own NLL), the perplexity ratio as an exponentiated paired delta, the rank correlation,
  and the refusal to merge runs from different commits.
- [x] **Real experiment run.** `scripts/02_policy_quality.py --config configs/phase10.yaml`, once
  per context, launched detached from a worktree pinned at the commit under test.
- [x] **Phase doc written.** This file.
- [x] **Committed and pushed.**

## What was measured, and what was fixed before the run

| Axis | Setting | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Documents | 12 windows of 256 tokens across two Project Gutenberg novels | Long, public-domain, and already verified by SHA-256 in `data/corpus/manifest.json`. PG-19-style text, **not** the PG-19 benchmark split, so no number here is comparable to a published PG-19 perplexity. |
| Scored tokens | 3,072 per condition, the *same* tokens at every context | Each window is a fixed book position; a run at context C puts the C tokens before it in the cache. Every comparison is paired, by condition and by context. |
| Policies | Rungs 2, 4, 5, 8 | Rung 3 is rung 2 without a sink on every prompt (Phase 2); rungs 6-7 are rung 5 bit for bit (Phase 4); rung 9 is exact by construction and decodes at 6.1–6.5× the full cache's time, so its perplexity is not measured. |
| Budgets | 75% to 6.25% | The study's sweep. |
| Contexts | 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K | Brief §B7.3 asks for perplexity per context length. |

Perplexity is read off the rows the KL was already computed from — the log-probability each
condition assigned to the token that actually came next — so it costs no extra decoding. The
effect reported is the **paired NLL delta against the full cache**, and the perplexity ratio it
exponentiates to. Its 95% CI is a bootstrap over the windows: the 256 tokens of one window share a
context and are not independent, and resampling them would make the interval several times too
narrow. `configs/phase10.yaml` sets no pass/fail bar, because the brief defines none for
perplexity and choosing one after Phase 9 would be choosing it to fit.

## 1. The answer: perplexity barely registers what a budget loses

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="../figures/p10_perplexity-dark.png">
  <img alt="NIAH retention against perplexity ratio for each policy and budget at 32K, and the perplexity ratio at the tightest budget across context lengths" src="../figures/p10_perplexity-light.png">
</picture>

At 32,768 tokens, NIAH retention for every condition
is already measured on the ladder (same model, block size and slot setting), so each point on the
left panel is one condition's two quality costs side by side.

**9 of
20 conditions lose at least a tenth of the
full cache's retrieval while their perplexity CI still includes no change at all.** The starkest is
the sliding window with a sink at a
25% budget: it keeps
24.4% of the full cache's NIAH
retrieval, and its perplexity is
1.024× the full cache's
(95% CI 0.995–1.055).
The same window at 75% keeps
62.5% of retrieval,
at a perplexity ratio of
1.008.

The ordering is not the problem. Across the 20
conditions, the NLL delta ranks them by NIAH loss with a Spearman correlation of
0.94 (teacher-forced KL:
0.89), mostly because both get worse as the
budget shrinks. The problem is the *size* of what perplexity sees. Most next-token predictions in running text lean
on nearby text (§3 finds the same thing from another direction), so removing three quarters of the
context changes little of the average, and the few tokens that needed the distant context are
diluted by the rest. This is
the failure that LongPPL (arXiv 2410.23771, ICLR 2025; see [related work](../RELATED_WORK.md))
describes and designs around. This phase measures it rather than adopting their fix after the fact.

**So a perplexity budget would badly mislead a reader of this study.** At
32,768 tokens, perplexity alone would put every
policy at every budget down to 25% within a few percent of the full cache (the table in §2), and the headline question — how
much *context* a budget retains — is exactly what it cannot see.

The 100% block-pool control reproduces the full cache's NLL to
0.0e+00 nats at every context, so none of the
deltas come from the block layout.

At 32,768 tokens,
6 of
20 conditions are worse than the full
cache with a CI that excludes "no change", and none of them at a budget above
12.5%.
2 read slightly *better*, both at
75%: Quest-style selection
(0.9969, CI
0.9943–1.0000)
and the int8 tier
(0.9966, CI
0.9943–0.9991).
**Treat these as noise, not a gain.** Across all
80 policy conditions at every context,
2 read better than the full cache with
an interval excluding no change — these two — which is about what a 2.5% one-sided miss rate
predicts by chance alone. Both upper bounds are within a thousandth of 1, and the two conditions
share nearly all of their selection (rung 8 is rung 5's selection with int8 cold blocks), so they
are not two independent observations. Phase 5 and Phase 7 made the same call about similar
apparent gains.

## 3. Across context

| Context | Full-cache perplexity | Mean NLL (nats) | Perplexity over the longest context | Windows worse than at the longest |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4,096 | 24.134 | 3.1836 | 1.084 | 9 / 12 |
| 8,192 | 22.781 | 3.1259 | 1.023 | 7 / 12 |
| 16,384 | 23.213 | 3.1447 | 1.043 | 9 / 12 |
| 32,768 | 22.261 | 3.1028 | reference |  |

**The corpus does reward long context, modestly.** The full cache's perplexity at
4,096 tokens is
1.084× its perplexity at
32,768 on the same scored tokens (95% CI
1.037–1.140;
9 of
12 windows worse). Beyond that first step it is not monotone
(the table has 16K reading worse than 8K), so no trend between 8K and 32K is claimed. That matters for reading everything below: if more
context barely helps the reference, removing context can barely hurt a policy, which is §1's
finding seen from the other side.

**A fixed budget fraction costs less perplexity as the context grows — the opposite of what
retrieval does.** Of the 13 conditions
whose cost is resolved at 4,096 tokens, **all
13** cost less at
32,768. The mechanism is the obvious one once seen:
most tokens are predicted from the text just before them, and 25% of 32K is still 8K tokens of
recent text, while 25% of 4K is 1K.

Phase 8's collapse test puts a number on it. Grouping each policy's NLL delta across contexts by the
budget fraction leaves a mean spread of
0.047 nats; grouping it by the
blocks kept leaves 0.036, so the blocks
kept hold perplexity 1.30× tighter. For
NIAH retrieval, [Phase 8](PHASE_8.md) found the reverse, with the fraction
2.7× tighter. Taken alone this collapse is
weak evidence: both spreads are only two to two and a half times the median half-width of a single
condition's interval (0.020 nats). The
every-condition trend above is the stronger evidence, and the two point the same way.

**So the two quality metrics disagree about scaling, not only about size.** A residency policy's
retrieval cost is a function of the share of the document it keeps; its perplexity cost is closer
to a function of how much recent text it keeps. A perplexity result measured at one context says
little about retrieval at that context, and less at any other.

## 4. What this changes

- **§B7.3 is now measured.** Long-document perplexity is reported for four rungs, five budgets and
  four contexts.
- **Perplexity is not a usable headline for this study.** Retrieval is what a residency policy
  loses, and perplexity dilutes it into the average. NIAH (and teacher-forced KL, which resolves
  far smaller effects per token) remain the study's quality measures.
- **This supports Phase 9's advice rather than resolving it.** Phase 9 found the 99% NIAH bar too
  fine for 300 prompts. A perplexity threshold would be the wrong substitute: it would pass
  conditions that lose most of their retrieval. If the headline needs a continuous metric, the
  candidate is teacher-forced KL, or a key-token perplexity in the LongPPL sense, and choosing one
  is an owner decision.
